330.title: Greet Phoebe (Romans 16)
330.hook: the letter ends with a list of people, many of them women, like Phoebe the deacon
330.howItsDone: Many churches remember Phoebe, Priscilla and Junia among the saints and early leaders, and in most traditions deacons serve the poor, help in worship and care for the practical life of the congregation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the weak and the strong at one table in Rome, and your line was welcome one another. Did you make someone who does things differently feel at home? Day three hundred thirty.

Most people skip the end of Romans. After the great chapters about grace and faith and nothing can separate us, chapter sixteen looks like the credits at the end of a movie: a long list of names nobody can pronounce. Greet this one. Greet that one. Salute the household of so-and-so. You reach for the remote. But stay for the credits. Some of the best stories in the whole letter are hiding in that list. And the very first name, before anyone else, belongs to a woman traveling from a port town near Corinth, probably with the letter itself in her bag.
screen: `THE CREDITS AT THE END.` → `A LIST NOBODY READS.` → `THE FIRST NAME: A WOMAN WITH THE LETTER.`

segments.voice: Paul writes, in the King James Bible: "I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea." Cenchreae was the eastern port of Corinth. Servant here is the Greek word diakonos, the word we get deacon from. It's the same word Paul uses for himself as a minister of the gospel, and even for Christ. Many scholars think Phoebe carried this letter to Rome, which means she may have been the first person to read it aloud there, and to answer questions about it. Paul asks the Romans to help her in whatever she needs, and he calls her a helper, a patron, of many, and of Paul himself. Then the list. Priscilla and Aquila, a wife and husband who, Paul says, risked their necks for him, and who host a church in their home. Mary, who worked hard. Andronicus and Junia, who were in prison with Paul, and whom he calls of note among the apostles. Tryphaena and Tryphosa, two women who labor in the Lord. Rufus's mother, who, Paul says, was a mother to him too. More than two dozen names, and around a third of them women. Even the secretary who wrote the words down pops up to say hello: I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you. Churches today differ on women's roles, so here's who says what. Many Protestant churches ordain women as deacons, and some as pastors. The early churches of the East had deaconesses, and some Orthodox churches are discussing restoring them. The Catholic Church ordains only men as deacons, and has been studying the question. But every church can read this list the same way: every name was a real someone.
screen: `PHOEBE, A DIAKONOS AT CENCHREAE.` · `SHE LIKELY CARRIED THE LETTER.` · `PRISCILLA, JUNIA, RUFUS'S MOTHER.` · `I TERTIUS, WHO WROTE THIS EPISTLE.` · then, large: `I COMMEND UNTO YOU PHEBE OUR SISTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a church worker by name. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people who keep a place of faith or care running, whose names rarely get said. The person who sets up chairs. The one who runs the food pantry. A choir director, a janitor, a nursery volunteer, a chaplain. If you don't belong to a church, think of anyone who serves quietly: a school secretary, a nurse, a crossing guard. Pick one. Say their name to yourself, the way Paul does: greet this one. Decide how you'll thank them. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Deacon. Diakonos in Greek: a servant, a minister. And Phoebe of Cenchreae, the first name in Paul's closing list, carries it.

Your line: every name is someone. Today, thank that one person by name, out loud or in writing. That's the end of Romans; tomorrow, we climb up and look back over the whole year. Day three hundred thirty.

original.note: Greek: servant, minister, deacon. used of Phoebe, of Paul, and of Christ.

trapdoor: what you thought: a deacon is a man who helps with the offering.
what it means: diakonos means servant or minister, and at the top of the closing list of Romans, with that title, is a woman: Phoebe.
what a scholar hears: Junia in 16:7 is a woman's name in the earliest manuscripts and church fathers; some later medieval and modern texts printed Junias, a man's name, though no such name is known.

331.title: The big lookout
331.hook: from a carpenter's town to Rome, from a seed to a creed: look back at the hill you've climbed
331.howItsDone: Many Christians mark the end of a season or a year with a time of looking back, sometimes called an examen or a year's review, giving thanks for what has passed before setting out again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of Romans, Phoebe the deacon and a list of names nobody reads, and your line was every name is someone. Did you thank someone by name? Day three hundred thirty-one.

Anyone who has hiked a long trail knows the moment. You've been looking at your boots for hours: the next rock, the next root, the next switchback. Then the path opens out onto a ledge, and you turn around. And there it all is. The parking lot, tiny. The river you crossed. The steep bit that nearly made you quit. You can't believe you walked all that. That's today. Three hundred thirty-one days ago you started at the bottom of this hill with one small word. Today we stop at the big lookout, turn around, and look back at the whole climb, before the path goes on.
screen: `LOOKING AT YOUR BOOTS FOR HOURS.` → `THE PATH OPENS ONTO A LEDGE.` → `YOU TURN AROUND.`

segments.voice: Camp one was first words. Amen, a word you'd said a thousand times. Grace, a gift you didn't earn. The Lord's Prayer, one line a day: our Father, thy kingdom come, daily bread, forgive us, deliver us. Agape. The cross. Easter morning, and the women at the tomb first. Camp two was the stories. A sower flinging seed on every kind of ground. A father running down the road. A girl in Nazareth, a carpenter's town nobody expected anything from. A road through Galilee, a last week in Jerusalem, and then Acts, the story carrying on, all the way to a shipwreck and to Rome. Camp three was the practices: ways to pray, Advent candles and the circle of the year, Sabbath, singing, giving, the sacraments, and a rule of life. Camp four was one Gospel, Mark, read in order, breathless, from the first line to the empty tomb and the young man's words: he's going ahead of you to Galilee. And camp five went deep: the Sermon on the Mount, the mystics, the whole family of churches, the creeds that grew from that seed, and these last three weeks, Paul's letter to Rome. From a mustard seed to a creed said by churches around the world. Paul, near the end of his own long road, wrote to his friends in Philippi, in the King James Bible: "forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark." The mark. The target. Remember hamartia, sin as missing the mark? Paul's answer isn't to stop aiming. It's to keep pressing on. That's where year two begins: the whole Bible, in order, from its first line.
screen: `CAMP ONE: FIRST WORDS.` · `CAMPS TWO AND THREE: STORIES, PRACTICES.` · `CAMP FOUR: MARK, IN ORDER.` · `CAMP FIVE: THE DEPTHS, AND ROMANS.` · then, large: `I PRESS TOWARD THE MARK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write the one line you'll carry into year two. Settle, and breathe. Let the whole year pass in front of you, like the view from the lookout. Which line stayed with you? Maybe one of the carries: fear buries things, but now, nothing can separate us. Maybe a verse. Maybe something you realized on your own, on an ordinary Tuesday. Don't choose the most impressive one. Choose the one that's actually yours. After the bell, write it down somewhere you'll see it. If you pray, you can give thanks for the climb so far. The bell holds the time.
The big lookout. The ledge at the end of year one, where you turn around, see the whole climb, and then face the path ahead.
Your line: the hill goes on. Today, put your one line where you'll see it tomorrow morning: on the fridge, the mirror, your phone. Year two starts at the very beginning. Day three hundred thirty-one.

original.note: Greek: the mark, the goal you keep your eyes on. the root of our word scope.

trapdoor: what you thought: the big lookout is the end of the climb.
what it means: a place to stop, turn around, see the whole year, and then face the path ahead.
what a scholar hears: in Philippians 3:14 Paul says he pursues the skopos, the mark, the same picture of aiming that hides in hamartia, missing the mark.
